paragraphs: Representing a moving scene with 4D Gaussian Splatting can produce high visual quality, but storing and rendering that representation is expensive. This paper identifies two sources of wasted work: many Gaussians represent only brief moments, and rendering processes Gaussians even when they contribute nothing to the current frame.

The proposed system, 4DGS-1K, addresses these problems separately. A Spatial-Temporal Variation Score guides pruning of short-lived Gaussians while encouraging the representation to describe motion using Gaussians that remain useful longer. An activity mask records which Gaussians contribute across consecutive frames, allowing rendering to avoid substantial computation on inactive elements.

On complex dynamic scenes, the authors report 41-fold lower storage requirements and ninefold faster rasterization than vanilla 4DGS, with comparable visual quality. The system exceeds 1,000 frames per second on modern GPUs. These findings show how reducing redundancy across time can improve both the compactness of a scene representation and the speed of producing its frames.
neurips-2025-1000-fps-4d-gaussian-splatt.tldr: 4DGS-1K reduces temporal redundancy to render dynamic scenes above 1,000 FPS while substantially cutting storage and preserving comparable visual quality.

paragraphs: Learning from unlabeled time series requires deciding which sequences or moments should have similar representations. Existing contrastive approaches can make those decisions without adequately capturing physical relationships or changes in a sequence’s behavior over time. AdaTS addresses this problem by making similarity assignments adaptive at both the sequence and temporal levels.

The method combines three mechanisms. Time-Frequency Coherence supplies a physics-guided measure of similarity. Ordinal consistency learning preserves relative similarity relationships between sequences, helping the learned representation retain which examples are more alike. Dynamic temporal assignments adapt to the non-stationarity of individual sequences, accounting for the fact that temporal behavior can change differently in different examples.

AdaTS is designed as a computationally efficient module that plugs into standard contrastive learning frameworks. Across diverse datasets and three existing frameworks, the authors report accuracy improvements of up to 13.7% and greater robustness when labels are scarce. The findings support adapting the learning signal to the structure of each time series instead of relying on a fixed treatment of similarity.
neurips-2025-adats-learning-adaptive-tim.tldr: AdaTS improves time-series representations by adapting contrastive similarities to physical correlations and sequence-specific changes over time.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback depends on evaluating the responses a language model produces. A conventional reward model provides these evaluations quickly, but can be vulnerable to reward hacking and unfamiliar inputs. Strong language-model judges offer better generalization in the setting described by the authors, although their higher inference cost makes frequent use expensive.

This paper combines the two evaluators through uncertainty-based routing. It expresses advantage estimation, the signal used in policy-gradient learning, as a classification problem over pairs of responses. That formulation provides a basis for measuring uncertainty: confident comparisons remain with the fast reward model, while uncertain comparisons are sent to the stronger judge.

On reward-model benchmarks, routing by uncertainty significantly outperforms calling the judge at random with the same spending. Downstream experiments also show improved online alignment. The result supports allocating costly judgments to comparisons where the cheaper evaluator is unsure, making the choice of when to ask for help part of the learning method.
neurips-2025-ask-a-strong-llm-judge-when.tldr: Routing uncertain reward-model comparisons to a stronger LLM judge improves evaluation and online alignment at a controlled judge-calling cost.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning uses image–text pairs to learn representations that connect the two modalities. When an image and its caption do not match well, the training signal can mix useful relationships with misleading ones. This paper examines that problem theoretically, studying two nonlinear encoders that are trained together using a contrastive loss.

The analysis follows how features change during training. It establishes how genuinely paired features become stronger while spurious features are suppressed, and shows how noisy or misaligned pairs produce mixed representations that harm generalization. The authors identify feature purity—the extent to which neurons learn the relevant features without this mixing—as a central factor in the analyzed learning process.

Recaptioning and filtering improve alignment between training images and text. Within the analysis, better alignment leads to purer learned features and improved generalization. Experiments on standard benchmarks support these theoretical insights. The contribution is an explanation connecting data-cleaning choices to internal representation learning and downstream performance, rather than treating data quality only as an empirical observation.
neurips-2025-contrastive-learning-with-d.tldr: The paper links image–text alignment to feature purity, explaining theoretically why recaptioning and filtering can improve contrastive-learning generalization.

paragraphs: Source-free domain adaptation updates a pretrained model for an unlabeled target domain without access to labeled source data. A common approach uses the model’s predictions as training labels, but those predictions can be unreliable after a domain change. DUET addresses this problem by controlling which predictions become supervision and how uncertainty influences adaptation.

Its pseudo-labeling rule combines two perspectives: the target model’s task-specific predictions and CLIP’s predictions as a domain-invariant perspective. Only samples on which they agree receive pseudo labels. Uncertain samples still contribute through consistency training, allowing representation learning without assigning them potentially noisy labels. Agreement therefore determines the form of learning applied to each sample.

DUET also uses a Tsallis mutual-information objective whose sensitivity to entropy changes according to an uncertainty-based adaptation index. This dynamically balances exploration and exploitation during training. The authors report state-of-the-art benchmark performance, with adaptation accuracy improvements of 1.6% on Office-Home, 1.4% on VisDA-C, and 2.9% on DomainNet-126. These results support combining selective supervision with uncertainty-responsive optimization.
neurips-2025-duet-dual-perspective-pseud.tldr: DUET adapts models to unlabeled domains using agreement-based pseudo labels, consistency training, and uncertainty-guided optimization.

paragraphs: Adversarial perturbations can cause multimodal language models to produce harmful responses. However, a perturbation optimized for a particular image and prompt, or a fixed dataset, may transfer poorly to unfamiliar inputs. This paper studies how to create a shared perturbation that remains effective across different images and prompts.

The approach models a distribution of possible inputs instead of optimizing only against a fixed collection of pairs. It uses a Laplace approximation to obtain a Gaussian representation with estimated mean and covariance parameters. Monte Carlo samples from that approximation then guide optimization of one input-agnostic perturbation across varied image–prompt combinations.

The authors report strong adversarial performance and transferability in experiments involving prevalent multimodal models and a range of images and prompts. The finding is that fitting an approximate input distribution can help reduce the overfitting associated with more narrowly optimized attacks. The reported universality concerns transfer across the evaluated settings; the method’s underlying representation remains an approximation of the potential input distribution.
neurips-2025-fit-the-distribution-cross-.tldr: Approximating the image–prompt input distribution helps train a shared adversarial perturbation that transfers across varied multimodal inputs.

paragraphs: Proving an inequality can involve rewriting an expression as a combination of components that are each non-negative. Finding the right decomposition is difficult to automate because it requires selecting and combining suitable theorems. IneqSearch turns that task into a structured search problem supported by both symbolic computation and a language model.

The system assigns complementary roles to its components. A symbolic solver handles deductive reasoning, while an LLM-based agent explores constructive routes toward a proof. Their shared objective is to discover theorem combinations that produce the required non-negative decomposition. This ties the language model’s exploration to explicit mathematical transformations that contribute to a proof.

IneqSearch also adds newly proven results to its theorem database through an iterative learning mechanism. This lets later proof searches draw on knowledge accumulated during earlier practice without human intervention. In an evaluation of 437 Olympiad-level inequalities, the system proves 342 and significantly outperforms existing methods. The findings support combining guided exploration, symbolic deduction, and a growing collection of reusable results.
neurips-2025-ineqsearch-hybrid-reasoning.tldr: IneqSearch combines symbolic deduction, LLM-guided exploration, and accumulated theorems to prove 342 of 437 evaluated Olympiad inequalities.

paragraphs: Designing a protein binder for a specific site requires generating a plausible interface: the geometry and interactions through which the binder meets its target. Existing structure-based generators struggle to produce interfaces with sufficient rationality and interpretability. RADiAnce addresses this by using known interfaces to guide the generation of new binders.

Retrieval and generation operate in a shared contrastive latent space, a learned representation used to connect relevant interfaces with a binding site. The framework retrieves suitable examples and incorporates them into a conditional latent diffusion generator. This arrangement makes retrieved interface knowledge part of the generation process and supports transferring interface patterns across different binder domains.

The reported experiments show significant improvements over baseline models in binding affinity and recovery of geometries and interactions. Additional results indicate that retrieving interfaces from peptides, antibodies, and protein fragments can improve generation for other domains. These findings support the usefulness of sharing interface knowledge across categories when designing new binders, with retrieval providing guidance for the generative model.
neurips-2025-latent-retrieval-augmented-.tldr: RADiAnce retrieves known protein interfaces in a shared latent space to guide binder generation and improve cross-domain design performance.

paragraphs: A correct reactive system must both avoid unwanted behavior and make progress toward its objectives. These requirements correspond to safety and liveness. Earlier neural model checking focused on ranking functions, which certify progress. This paper extends the approach to inductive invariants, which support proofs that unsafe behavior cannot occur.

The proposed neural certificate represents both kinds of evidence in one architecture. Given a system and a linear temporal logic specification, learning and checking alternate toward a provably sound certificate. The checking component matters because the resulting assurance comes from a verified mathematical certificate, rather than simply from a neural network predicting that the system behaves correctly.

The architecture also supports training with constraint solvers, accelerating earlier neural model-checking approaches based on gradient descent. On evaluated SystemVerilog tasks covering pure liveness and combined safety and liveness, the authors report speedups of orders of magnitude over state-of-the-art model checkers. The method therefore broadens the properties neural model checking can verify while improving efficiency on the tested verification problems.
neurips-2025-let-a-neural-network-be-you.tldr: A joint neural certificate supports formally checked safety and liveness proofs, with large speedups on evaluated SystemVerilog verification tasks.

paragraphs: Planning for multiple agents requires considering combinations of their actions. That joint action space can grow exponentially with the number of agents, making Monte Carlo Tree Search expensive to expand and explore. MALinZero addresses this difficulty by exploiting low-dimensional structure in the returns associated with joint actions.

The method represents those returns through a contextual linear bandit formulation and develops LinUCT, a confidence-bound rule for tree search in that smaller space. Its convex, smooth losses emphasize better joint actions while mitigating representational limitations. This changes how the search balances exploring uncertain choices and exploiting promising ones without treating every joint action as an unrelated option.

The paper analyzes regret for low-dimensional reward functions and gives a joint-action selection algorithm with a one-minus-one-over-e approximation guarantee for a submodular objective. On matrix games, SMAC, and SMACv2, the authors report state-of-the-art results, faster learning, and better performance than model-based and model-free baselines. The theoretical claims concern the specified reward structure and objective, while the benchmarks demonstrate practical planning benefits.
neurips-2025-malinzero-efficient-low-dim.tldr: MALinZero uses low-dimensional joint-action representations to make multi-agent tree search more efficient and improve benchmark performance.

paragraphs: A retrieval query can combine several images and textual conditions, requiring a system to preserve particular details as well as overall meaning. Existing datasets often cover only one language, one image, or one condition. MERIT expands this setting with 320,000 queries and 135,000 products spanning five languages and seven product categories.

Experiments on the dataset identify a recurring weakness: existing models concentrate on global semantics while overlooking individual conditions. The authors propose Coral, a fine-tuning framework for pretrained multimodal language models, to address this. Embedding reconstruction helps preserve fine-grained conditions, while contrastive learning develops a representation of the query’s broader meaning.

Coral achieves a reported 45.9% performance improvement over conventional approaches on MERIT, with generalization assessed on eight established retrieval benchmarks. Together, the dataset and method make it possible to study retrieval that depends on several interleaved requirements. The results suggest that preserving specific conditions and learning overall semantic similarity are complementary needs in this more expressive query setting.
neurips-2025-merit-multilingual-semantic.tldr: MERIT benchmarks multilingual retrieval with multiple interleaved conditions, while Coral improves retrieval by preserving both detailed requirements and global meaning.

paragraphs: Many multimodal language models encode an image into a fixed collection of visual tokens before reasoning begins. This static representation limits their ability to refine visual understanding as the task develops. The paper introduces an inference-time framework in which visual processing proceeds iteratively and a verifier guides the reasoning process.

The framework casts this process as a Markov Decision Process. A reasoner proposes visual actions, while a verifier evaluates them and decides when reasoning should stop. The verifier is trained with multi-step Direct Preference Optimization. To support training, the authors introduce VTS, containing both supervised reasoning trajectories and preference-labeled comparisons between reasoning sequences.

The authors report significant improvements over existing approaches across diverse visual reasoning benchmarks, alongside more interpretable and visually grounded reasoning. The contribution connects decisions about what visual processing to perform with decisions about whether enough reasoning has occurred. These findings support dynamic visual inference as a promising way to make image understanding more responsive to the context of a particular task.
neurips-2025-multi-step-visual-reasoning.tldr: Verifier-guided visual actions let multimodal models refine their understanding during inference, improving accuracy and grounding on visual reasoning benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reasoning over several images requires understanding relationships across the sequence, including positional relationships that do not arise in a single-image task. Existing multimodal reinforcement-learning methods often focus on spatial reasoning within one image. PeRL develops a training approach for interleaved multimodal tasks, with particular attention to reasoning across multiple images.

Its multi-stage strategy combines broader exploration with more selective use of generated learning trajectories. Permuting image sequences exposes the model to varied positional relationships and greater spatial diversity. A rollout filtering and resampling mechanism then focuses training on trajectories that contribute most to learning useful behavior. These mechanisms address complementary parts of the exploration–exploitation trade-off.

The evaluation covers five multi-image benchmarks and three single-image benchmarks. The authors report substantial improvements over R1-related and interleaved vision-language baselines, reaching state-of-the-art performance on multi-image tasks while retaining comparable single-image performance. The results suggest that explicitly varying image order and selecting informative training trajectories can improve more complex visual reasoning without sacrificing the tested single-image capability.
neurips-2025-perl-permutation-enhanced-r.tldr: PeRL combines image-sequence permutations with selective reinforcement-learning rollouts to improve multi-image reasoning while preserving comparable single-image performance.

paragraphs: Synthetic images can expand training data for object detection, where obtaining large annotated datasets is expensive. Their usefulness depends on whether generated objects match the intended content and positions. Existing generation approaches can suffer from mismatches and semantic leakage, where textual cues affect regions beyond their intended locations.

ReCon improves control within the diffusion generation process. Region-guided rectification uses feedback from a pretrained perception model to correct regions that are being generated incorrectly. Region-aligned cross-attention strengthens the correspondence between each image region and its associated textual cues. Together, these components address both local generation mistakes and the alignment of meaning with spatial position.

The authors report improved image quality and trainability of the synthetic data, along with consistent object-detection gains across datasets, backbone architectures, and data scales. Trainability matters because visually plausible images must also provide useful learning signals for a detector. The findings connect better control during generation with the downstream value of generated examples as training data.
neurips-2025-recon-region-controllable-d.tldr: ReCon corrects generated image regions and aligns them with text cues to produce more useful synthetic training data for object detection.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models learn from fixed training datasets, while the visual world continues to change. This creates a gap between their stored knowledge and newer visual information. The paper introduces LiveVQA to examine two responses to that gap: seeking current information when needed and updating a model with new visual knowledge.

LiveVQA contains 107,143 samples across 12 categories, drawn from news articles, video platforms, and academic publications. It supports evaluation of information beyond a model’s knowledge boundary and of methods intended to help models handle that information. Benchmarking 17 multimodal models reveals substantial performance gaps on content beyond their training cutoffs.

Tool-assisted or agentic visual seeking produces a reported average improvement of 327% in the evaluated setting. The authors also study parameter-efficient fine-tuning, examining the balance between adapter capacity and model capability when incorporating new knowledge. The work therefore provides both an evaluation resource and evidence about complementary ways to address stale visual knowledge: external information seeking and updates to the model.
neurips-2025-seeking-and-updating-with-l.tldr: LiveVQA measures gaps in current visual knowledge and evaluates information seeking and parameter-efficient updates as ways to address them.

paragraphs: Prediction-driven optimization must account for errors that affect whether a decision is feasible, as well as errors that affect its value. This paper studies contextual stochastic linear optimization with inequality constraints containing uncertain, predicted parameters. It handles that uncertainty using context-dependent uncertainty sets, which can be constructed through methods such as conformal prediction.

Given an uncertainty-set method, the authors define SPO-RC, a loss that evaluates predictions of objective parameters through their decision errors while accounting for feasibility. They also introduce the convex surrogate SPO-RC+ and prove Fisher consistency with the original loss. This provides a theoretical connection between optimizing the surrogate and the intended decision-focused objective.

The training approach can retain only examples whose true constraint parameters fall inside their uncertainty sets. Because this truncation changes the sample distribution, importance reweighting corrects the resulting selection bias. Experiments on fractional knapsack and alloy production show effective handling of constraint uncertainty, with further improvements possible from combining truncation and reweighting. The contribution links robust constraints, learnable losses, and training-data selection.
neurips-2025-smart-surrogate-losses-for-.tldr: SPO-RC+ trains predictions for optimization with uncertain constraints using a feasibility-sensitive surrogate and bias-corrected data selection.

paragraphs: Linguistic steganography hides a secret message inside generated text. The amount of information that fits is constrained by the limited entropy available during text generation. A low payload can require longer texts or more transmissions, increasing opportunities for suspicion. StegoZip approaches this capacity problem by processing the secret message before it is embedded.

The framework uses large language models in two complementary stages. Semantic redundancy pruning extracts a reduced representation of the message, and index-based compression coding turns that representation into compact binary codes. The aim is to reduce the space required for the secret itself, complementing previous work that focused on using the generated text’s available entropy more efficiently.

When combined with state-of-the-art steganographic methods under lossless decoding, StegoZip delivers 2.5 times the baseline payload with comparable practical processing time. The authors also report maintained provable content security and improved covertness through reduced transmission needs. These claims distinguish recovering the message and protecting its content from the operational benefit of carrying more information per transmission.
neurips-2025-stegozip-enhancing-linguist.tldr: StegoZip compresses secret messages before embedding, achieving 2.5 times the baseline payload under lossless decoding with comparable processing time.

paragraphs: Low-rank adaptation fine-tunes pretrained models through compact parameter updates, but its performance can lag behind full fine-tuning. StelLA investigates whether better use of the geometry of low-rank updates can improve adaptation. Its central change is to separate the directions an adapter uses from the scaling applied within those directions.

The update has three factors, U, S, and V-transpose, resembling a singular value decomposition. U and V represent output and input subspaces, while S supplies scaling. The method keeps U and V on the Stiefel manifold, preserving orthonormality during training. A modular optimization design converts Euclidean optimizers into Riemannian ones so that updates respect these geometric constraints.

The authors evaluate commonsense reasoning, mathematics and code generation, image classification, and image generation. Across these tasks, they report superior performance over recent state-of-the-art LoRA variants. The contribution is a geometry-aware way to learn compact adaptation subspaces while maintaining compatibility with existing fine-tuning pipelines. The results support its advantage over the tested LoRA alternatives.
neurips-2025-stella-subspace-learning-in.tldr: StelLA improves low-rank adaptation by separating subspaces from scaling and preserving orthonormal subspace geometry throughout training.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn which choices are better through noisy pairwise preferences. Evaluators may introduce systematic bias, so the feedback can reflect more than the quality of the choices being compared. This paper develops algorithms that account for such bias while minimizing regret, the cost accumulated from making inferior choices during learning.

The authors first consider known evaluator biases. Even then, separating bias from observed feedback is difficult. They construct an unbiased performance estimator and a bias-sensitive algorithm, with a regret analysis showing that feedback matching or opposing ground truth can reduce regret in the analyzed setting. Thus, biased feedback can still contain useful information when its structure is accounted for.

For unknown biases, the estimation problem is non-convex and difficult to solve in closed form. An extended algorithm uses block coordinate descent and achieves the same order of regret as the known-bias case, with bounded error. Experiments report regret reductions of up to 86.9% against baselines, supporting explicit treatment of evaluator bias in preference-based learning.
neurips-2025-tackling-biased-evaluators-.tldr: Bias-sensitive dueling-bandit algorithms use evaluator bias information, or estimate it, to reduce regret when learning from pairwise preferences.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation assigns text-described categories throughout an image, requiring predictions at the pixel level. Test-time adaptation has received attention for image classification, but this paper argues that segmentation needs its own adaptation design. The proposed Multi-Level and Multi-Prompt method, MLMP, adapts vision-language models using the test inputs themselves.

MLMP minimizes entropy across both global and local predictions. It combines features from intermediate vision-encoder layers and uses multiple text-prompt templates, applying its objective at the global classification token and individual pixels. The method requires no additional training data or labels, remains effective with one test sample, and is presented as a plug-and-play addition to segmentation networks.

The authors also introduce an evaluation suite covering nine segmentation datasets, 15 common synthetic corruptions, and real and rendered domain shifts, totaling 87 scenarios. Their experiments report consistent, significant improvements over directly adopting classification-oriented adaptation baselines. The findings support designing adaptation around segmentation’s spatial predictions and multiple feature levels, while the benchmark provides a broader basis for evaluating those adaptations.
neurips-2025-test-time-adaptation-of-vis.tldr: MLMP adapts open-vocabulary segmentation models at test time using multiple feature levels and prompts, improving results across a broad shift benchmark.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how visual information reaches the text-processing part of a multimodal model. It compares native models trained from scratch to generate both images and text with non-native models adapted from language models or restricted to text generation. The focus is the internal flow of information during image-understanding tasks.

The authors find greater separation between image and text embeddings in the residual stream of native models. They also identify different communication patterns. Non-native models distribute visual-to-text communication across multiple image tokens, while models trained natively for joint generation tend to concentrate it in one token immediately following the image. That token functions as a narrow communication point.

Removing this token substantially harms image understanding in the studied models, providing evidence that the concentrated pathway matters for performance. Targeted interventions at the token also reliably steer image semantics and downstream text with fine-grained control. These findings connect an internal information-flow pattern with both a vulnerability to ablation and an opportunity to influence the model’s interpretation.
neurips-2025-the-narrow-gate-localized-i.tldr: Native image-and-text generators tend to channel visual information through one post-image token whose removal or modification strongly affects understanding.

paragraphs: Linear recurrent models have favorable theoretical scaling with sequence length, but practical speed depends on GPU kernels. Existing Flash Linear Attention parallelizes across sequence chunks, yet limited chunk sizes require many intermediate states to be stored in GPU memory. Moving and storing those states creates substantial overhead, especially during long-context pretraining.

Tiled Flash Linear Attention introduces additional parallelism within each chunk. This enables arbitrarily large chunks and higher arithmetic intensity, addressing the memory and input/output costs of the earlier formulation. The authors apply the algorithm to mLSTM, the matrix-memory version of xLSTM, and introduce a variant with a sigmoid input gate and reduced computation.

The modified mLSTM achieves faster kernel runtimes at equal language-modeling performance in the reported evaluation. Speed benchmarks show the new kernels outperforming highly optimized Flash Attention, Linear Attention, and Mamba kernels. The contribution demonstrates how changing the organization of GPU computation can turn a sequence model’s theoretical efficiency into practical runtime improvements for long-context modeling primitives.
neurips-2025-tiled-flash-linear-attentio.tldr: TFLA adds parallelism within sequence chunks to deliver faster mLSTM kernels and reduce the memory overhead of linear recurrent computation.

paragraphs: Unsupervised reinforcement-learning pretraining develops behavior before the eventual task rewards are available. One approach encourages a policy to visit a diverse range of states by maximizing state-distribution entropy. This principle is well studied for individual agents, but multiple agents introduce alternative formulations and additional challenges in turning the objective into practical learning.

The paper characterizes those alternative formulations and examines their theoretical difficulty. It highlights that a formulation can be tractable in theory yet remain difficult to solve in practice. To address practical settings, the authors propose a scalable, decentralized policy-search algorithm using a trust-region approach, connecting the analysis to a method for learning agent policies.

Numerical evaluations support the theoretical findings and assess state-entropy maximization in challenging multi-agent domains. Among the objectives considered, mixture entropy provides a particularly strong balance between tractability and performance. The contribution is therefore both conceptual and algorithmic: it clarifies choices in defining unsupervised multi-agent exploration and supplies a practical approach for optimizing a promising formulation.
neurips-2025-towards-principled-unsuperv.tldr: The paper analyzes multi-agent state-entropy objectives and introduces decentralized policy search, finding mixture entropy offers a strong practical trade-off.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing aims to correct or update a language model without fully retraining it. Evaluating an edit requires checking more than the changed fact: related knowledge may need to change, while other knowledge should remain stable. UniEdit broadens evaluation beyond narrow domains and limited checks of these ripple effects.

The benchmark draws editing samples from knowledge graphs, selecting entities across 25 domains within five major categories. Its Neighborhood Multi-hop Chain Sampling algorithm builds surrounding subgraphs to capture relationships relevant to evaluating generality and locality. Proprietary language models convert those subgraphs into natural-language material with varied syntax, making the structured knowledge usable for language-model evaluation.

Statistical analysis supports the benchmark’s scale, breadth, and diversity. Experiments across multiple language models and editing methods examine strengths and weaknesses across knowledge domains and evaluation criteria. The main contribution is an evaluation resource that treats knowledge edits as changes within a network of relationships, enabling a broader assessment of whether an editor updates the intended knowledge and handles its surrounding consequences appropriately.
neurips-2025-uniedit-a-unified-knowledge.tldr: UniEdit evaluates language-model knowledge editing across diverse domains and the related facts that edits may affect.

paragraphs: Keypoint estimation locates meaningful points in images, but training usually requires extensive annotation. This paper studies a weak-shot setting: labeled base classes support learning keypoints for multiple novel classes whose images have no labels. The central question is what knowledge can transfer across classes without requiring new keypoint annotations.

The proposed answer combines keyness and correspondence. Keyness compares pixels within a local region to identify which is more suitable as a keypoint, guiding candidate points toward local maxima. Correspondence compares pixels across paired images to determine whether they represent the same semantic part. Enforcing consistency between corresponding locations helps activate keypoints in the novel classes.

Both forms of knowledge concern comparisons between entities, which the authors describe as class-agnostic and transferable across classes. Experiments and analyses on the large-scale MP-100 benchmark demonstrate favorable weak-shot keypoint performance. The findings support transferring local point-selection behavior together with cross-image semantic relationships, giving unlabeled novel classes two complementary sources of guidance from labeled base classes.
neurips-2025-weak-shot-keypoint-estimati.tldr: Transferring local keypoint preferences and cross-image correspondences enables keypoint learning for unlabeled novel classes using labeled base classes.
